opus-5.5.text:
I think the difference is less about the model and more about the whole loop around it. If you look at the earlier agent systems, a lot of them were basically demos. You had a model, a prompt that said "you are an agent," a few tools stitched together, and maybe a planner on top. They looked impressive in a video, but if you ran them on a real task for thirty minutes, they would drift, lose context, call the wrong tool, or confidently declare success when nothing had actually worked.

What changed with something like Claude Code is that the agent is embedded in a real working environment. It has a file system, a terminal, tests, git, and actual feedback from the world. When it writes code, the code runs or it doesn't. When it edits a file, it can read it back. That closed loop of action, observation, and correction is what makes it industrial-grade instead of a toy. The model isn't just generating plausible text about doing work. It's doing the work and being checked by reality at every step.

The second big difference is reliability over long horizons. Early systems were optimized for single-turn intelligence: can the model answer this question well? An industrial agent needs to sustain coherence across hundreds of steps. That means context management, deciding what to remember and what to summarize, knowing when to stop and ask the user, and recovering from its own mistakes. Those capabilities weren't really trained for before. Now they are, through reinforcement learning on real agentic trajectories, and you can feel it in how the models behave.

The third is the engineering around permissions, safety, and trust. When you let an agent touch someone's codebase or their machine, you need clear boundaries. What can it do without asking, what's reversible, what isn't. That product layer sounds boring, but it's exactly what lets people actually hand over real tasks instead of just playing with it.

So I'd say the earlier systems asked, "Can a language model pretend to be an agent?" The current generation asks, "Can a model be trusted to do a real job end to end?" Those are very different questions, and answering the second one forced changes in training, in infrastructure, and in product design all at once.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the clearest way to put it is that earlier agent systems were demos, and what you see now in Claude Code or OpenClaude is infrastructure. Those sound like degrees of the same thing, but they're really different in kind.

Take the 2023 generation of agents, the AutoGPT-style systems. The architecture was essentially a loop wrapped around a model that was never trained to be in that loop. You'd prompt it to plan, prompt it to pick a tool, parse whatever came back, and hope the next step made sense. The model had no native sense of what a tool call was, no reliable way to recover when a call failed, and no stable notion of when it was done. So you got these long, meandering trajectories where the agent would do something clever on step three and then completely lose the thread by step twelve. People called that an agent, but honestly the agency was mostly in the scaffolding, and the scaffolding was fragile.

The industrial-grade systems flipped the relationship. The model itself is trained end to end on long-horizon tasks, with tool use, with real environments, with reinforcement learning on whether the task actually got completed. So the model learns things that no prompt can give you: when to read more context before acting, when a test failure means your fix was wrong versus the test was flaky, when to stop and ask rather than guess. The harness around it, the permission model, the file tools, the way context is managed over hours of work, that's engineered, but it's engineered to match what the model can actually do, rather than to compensate for what it can't.

The second difference is the error profile. An early agent was right maybe sixty or seventy percent of the time on individual steps, and if you multiply that over thirty steps you get something that almost never finishes a real task. Industrial agents are built around the assumption that they will run for a very long time, across many files, many commands, and the failure rate per step has to be low enough that the compound result is still useful. That's not a prompt engineering problem. That's a training and evaluation problem, and it's why the leap happened at the model level, not at the framework level.

And the third thing, which I think people underrate, is accountability. A demo agent could do something surprising and you'd laugh and tweet it. A coding agent that touches your production repository has to be predictable about what it will and won't do, has to report failures faithfully, has to not quietly narrow the task when it gets hard. That reliability of behavior is itself a capability, and it's one the earlier systems never had because nobody was optimizing for it.

So when I say fundamentally different, I mean the earlier systems were showing that a language model could be made to look like an agent. The current systems are language models that have actually become agents.

astra-6.text:
I think the fundamental difference is whether the agent can reliably carry a task through to completion. Earlier systems often demonstrated a loop: the model makes a plan, calls a tool, looks at the result, and decides what to do next. That can produce an impressive demo, but it doesn’t necessarily hold up when the task takes many steps or something unexpected happens.

For an industrial-grade agent, that loop is only the starting point. It needs to work within a real environment, keep track of what it has done, recover from failures, and verify whether the result actually satisfies the request. In coding, producing a plausible patch is different from understanding the repository, making the change, running the relevant checks, and correcting problems those checks reveal.

So I wouldn’t say the distinction is simply that one uses tools and the other doesn’t. It’s that the model and the surrounding system work together well enough that you can delegate meaningful work. The important question shifts from “Can it perform this action?” to “Can I trust it to finish this task, and tell me accurately when it can’t?”

sol-6.1.text:
I think the fundamental difference is whether the agent can reliably carry a task through to completion in a real working environment. Earlier systems often demonstrated a loop: make a plan, call a tool, observe the result, and repeat. That can look impressive in a demo, but the user still has to intervene frequently.

With an industrial-grade agent, that loop is only the starting point. It needs to understand an existing codebase, choose the right tools, manage context over a long task, recover when something fails, and verify its own changes. It also needs clear permission boundaries so you can let it work without approving every small action.

So I wouldn’t say the distinction is simply that one uses tools and the other doesn’t. It’s the amount of responsibility you can actually delegate. Can you give it an objective and trust it to make progress, check the result, and tell you honestly what remains unresolved? That’s the important shift.
